Here is how it is happening. The reservation's boundaries were set by Congress, and a 1927 law says they cannot change except by an Act of Congress. Trump's own 2025 border memo excluded Federal Indian Reservations. The administration is building anyway.

The border runs through the middle of the nation. About 34,000 O'odham live in the US and 3,000 in Mexico. They cross to attend funerals, run sacred pilgrimages, visit family, and haul water. A solid wall would make much of that impossible.

This land already has border infrastructure. In 2006 the O'odham agreed to vehicle barriers that stop cars and trucks but let tribal members cross on foot with ID. Trump wants to replace that with a double line of 30-foot steel panels.

The plan covers more than 60 miles of the reservation. About 19 miles of 30-foot primary wall, 42 miles of secondary barrier, plus stadium-style lights, surveillance cameras, fiber-optic cable, and new patrol roads cut through the desert.
